newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: OECD official sees little Australia rate cut scope.
newsitem.headline: OECD official sees little Australia rate cut scope.

text.p: Australia would risk an acceleration of its inflation rate if it eased monetary policy again, a senior OECD official said on Thursday.
"I think there is no or very little scope for further monetary relaxation," OECD chief administrator with responsibilty for Australia Helmut Ziegelschmidt told Australian Broadcasting Corp radio.

"The economy is already growing along potential output and the capacity slack of the economy that existed in the past has been eliminated, so there's no room for further stimulation of the economy without risking acceleration of inflation," he said.
The Reserve Bank of Australia has cut official cash rates a total of 200 basis points, to 5.5 percent, in four equal cuts from July 1996 to May 23 this year.
Australia's consumer price index rose 0.2 percent in the March quarter for an annual inflation rate of 1.3 percent.
Underlying consumer prices, the measure preferred by policymakers, rose 0.4 percent in the quarter to be up 2.1 percent over the year.
Ziegelschmidt said the major economic problem currently facing Australia was its continually high unemployment rate.

But he said further interest rate cuts would have little positive impact on the unemployment rate, which has been stuck around 8.5 percent since the Liberal-National coalition won office in March 1996.
Ziegelschmidt said employment was unlikely to pick up for some time.
"I think what has to be done is to continue with structural reforms and one will see the benefits unfortunately only over the medium term, so one has to be patient I'm afraid," he said.
The Organisation for Economic Development (OECD) last week released a report on the Australian economy, forecasting GDP growth of 3.5 percent in calendar 1997.
However, the report had been overtaken by a number of significant economic events, including a monetary policy easing and budget cuts, since the time it was prepared.
